title: Chapter 7 Mastery Quiz: Research Methods in Cognitive Neuroscience
description: Test your mastery of structural and functional imaging (CT, MRI, DTI, PET, fMRI), electrophysiology (EEG, ERPs, MEG), and causal interventions (TMS, optogenetics).

questions.question: What is the primary physical basis of image contrast in Computerized Tomography (CT) scans?

options.text: Differential tissue absorption of rotating X-ray beams based on physical density
Resonance frequency of hydrogen protons in a magnetic field
Positron-electron annihilation gamma rays
Detection of magnetic fields generated by dendrites

questions.explanation: CT scanners use rotating X-ray tubes; dense structures like bone attenuate X-rays strongly (appearing bright white).

questions.question: In a T1-weighted structural MRI scan, how do fat (myelin) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) typically appear?

options.text: Fat/myelin is bright (hyperintense); CSF is dark (hypointense)
CSF is bright white; fat/myelin is pitch black
Both fat and CSF appear identical shades of green
T1 scans show only blood vessels, with no brain tissue visible

questions.explanation: T1-weighted MRI provides anatomical contrast where lipid-rich white matter appears bright and fluid-filled CSF appears dark.

questions.question: What does Fractional Anisotropy (FA) in Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) measure?

options.text: The degree to which water diffusion is directionally constrained along myelinated axonal tracts
The rate of glucose consumption in tumor cells
The speed of red blood cells in the carotid artery
The electrical resistance of the skull bone

questions.explanation: FA quantifies how strongly directional water diffusion is; values near 1 indicate highly aligned, intact white matter tracts.

questions.question: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) detects brain activity by recording:

options.text: Collinear pairs of 511 keV gamma rays emitted when emitted positrons annihilate with tissue electrons
Infrared heat radiated by the cerebral cortex
Auditory clicks generated by open ion channels
Changes in scalp electrical conductivity

questions.explanation: Positron-electron annihilation produces two 511 keV photons traveling in opposite directions, detected by PET coincidence circuits.

questions.question: What does the BOLD acronym stand for in functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI)?

options.text: Blood Oxygen Level-Dependent
Brain Oscillation Longitudinal Detector
Basal Output Linearity Differentiation
Binary Optical Laser Diffraction

questions.explanation: BOLD stands for Blood Oxygen Level-Dependent contrast, which reflects changes in local blood oxygenation.

questions.question: Why does an increase in oxygenated hemoglobin increase the MR signal in fMRI?

options.text: Oxygenated hemoglobin is diamagnetic and does not distort the local magnetic field, unlike paramagnetic deoxygenated hemoglobin
Oxygenated hemoglobin emits radiofrequency bursts on its own
It physically heats up the brain tissue by 5 degrees
It destroys white matter myelin sheaths

questions.explanation: Deoxygenated hemoglobin is paramagnetic and creates field inhomogeneities; displacing it with diamagnetic oxyhemoglobin enhances MR signal.

questions.question: What is the typical time latency for the fMRI Hemodynamic Response Function (HRF) to reach its peak following neural activity?

options.text: 4 to 6 seconds
1 millisecond
30 minutes
24 hours

questions.explanation: Because vascular dilation is slow, the hemodynamic response rises gradually, peaking approximately 4 to 6 seconds after neural firing.

questions.question: The primary disadvantage of fMRI compared to EEG is its:

options.text: Poor temporal resolution (seconds vs. milliseconds)
Poor spatial resolution
Requirement for high doses of ionizing radiation
Inability to image living humans

questions.explanation: fMRI is limited by hemodynamic delay (temporal resolution of 1-3 seconds), whereas EEG tracks electrical events in milliseconds.

questions.question: What is the fundamental logic of 'Cognitive Subtraction' in neuroimaging experimental design?

options.text: Subtracting baseline control task activation from experimental task activation to isolate a specific mental process
Subtracting the patient's age from their IQ score
Subtracting heart rate from breathing rate to calculate sleep depth
Deleting all voxel data that contains white matter

questions.explanation: Cognitive subtraction isolates the neural correlate of a specific process by contrasting tasks that differ by only that operation.

questions.question: What is the primary electrical source recorded by scalp EEG electrodes?

options.text: Summed postsynaptic potentials of cortical pyramidal neurons aligned perpendicular to the scalp
Action potentials in single cranial nerves
Calcium influx in cerebellar Purkinje cells only
Blood pulsing through cerebral capillary beds

questions.explanation: EEG measures extracellular dipoles generated by synchronized postsynaptic potentials in perpendicularly oriented pyramidal neurons.

questions.question: What mathematical dilemma describes the impossibility of uniquely determining the 3D intracranial source of a scalp EEG signal without assumptions?

options.text: The Inverse Problem
The Forward Paradox
The Nyquist Theorem
Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle

questions.explanation: The Inverse Problem: infinitely many internal current source configurations can theoretically generate the same voltage pattern on the scalp surface.

questions.question: In Event-Related Potential (ERP) research, the N400 component is reliably elicited by:

options.text: Semantic anomalies or unexpected words that violate linguistic context (e.g., 'The pizza was too hot to cry')
Loud sudden auditory clicks in complete darkness
Viewing a familiar human face
Entering Stage N3 slow-wave sleep

questions.explanation: Discovered by Kutas and Hillyard (1980), the N400 is a negative deflection peaking at ~400 ms triggered by semantic incongruity.

questions.question: The N170 ERP component is electrophysiologically specialized for the cognitive processing of:

options.text: Human faces
Geometric triangles
High-pitched musical tones
Painful thermal heat stimuli

questions.explanation: The N170 is a negative occipitotemporal deflection peaking at ~170 ms that is significantly larger for human faces than other visual stimuli.

questions.question: Magnetoencephalography (MEG) detects minute magnetic fields generated by neural currents using which specialized cryogenic sensors?

options.text: SQUIDs (Superconducting Quantum Interference Devices)
Geiger counters
Photomultiplier tubes
Zinc sulfide scintillators

questions.explanation: MEG uses superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs) bathed in liquid helium to detect ultra-faint biomagnetic fields.

questions.question: Why cannot neuroimaging techniques like fMRI and EEG alone prove that a brain region is causally necessary for a behavior?

options.text: They are purely correlational; a brain region can activate during a task without being functionally required to perform it
They only record signals from dead tissue
They alter the subject's DNA during scanning
Their sensors are incapable of detecting brain waves

questions.explanation: Correlational imaging demonstrates co-occurrence, but causal intervention (lesion, TMS, optogenetics) is required to establish necessity.

questions.question: How does Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) temporarily disrupt cortical processing to create a 'virtual lesion'?

options.text: A fluctuating magnetic field induces a localized electrical current that depolarizes cortical neurons, introducing neural noise
It permanently freezes blood vessels in the scalp
It destroys the myelin sheaths of target neurons
It creates a temporary vacuum inside the skull

questions.explanation: TMS uses electromagnetic induction to fire neurons synchronously, disrupting coordinated computation and mimicking a focal reversible lesion.

questions.question: In optogenetics, what is Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2)?

options.text: A light-gated cation channel activated by blue light that depolarizes and excites neurons
A light-gated chloride pump activated by yellow light that inhibits neurons
A radioactive isotope injected to measure dopamine receptors
A hormone produced by the adrenal medulla during stress

questions.explanation: ChR2 is a microbial opsin that opens in response to ~470 nm blue light, allowing positive ions in to trigger action potentials.

questions.question: Which optogenetic opsin is activated by yellow light to pump chloride ions into neurons, thereby silencing their electrical activity?

options.text: Halorhodopsin (NpHR)
Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2)
Melanopsin
Rhodopsin

questions.explanation: Halorhodopsin (NpHR) is an inward chloride pump activated by yellow light (~580 nm) that hyperpolarizes and silences neurons.

questions.question: A 'double dissociation' in neuropsychology is crucial because it provides definitive evidence that:

options.text: Two cognitive functions rely on separate, independent neural systems
Both brain hemispheres have identical cognitive capacities
A single brain lesion always impairs all sensory modalities equally
Memory and language share the exact same cortical neurons

questions.explanation: A double dissociation (Patient 1 impaired on task A but normal on B; Patient 2 normal on A but impaired on B) proves modular independence.

questions.question: Which method would be ideal for measuring dopamine receptor occupancy of an experimental antipsychotic drug in humans?

options.text: PET with a radiolabeled dopamine receptor ligand (e.g., [11C]-Raclopride)
Structural T1-weighted MRI
Scalp EEG power spectral analysis
Computerized Tomography (CT)

questions.explanation: PET radioligand binding assays directly quantify pharmacological receptor displacement and occupancy in vivo.

questions.question: Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) applied to the Left Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex is FDA-approved for treating:

options.text: Treatment-resistant Major Depressive Disorder
Acute bacterial meningitis
Spinal cord transection
Complete optic nerve atrophy

questions.explanation: High-frequency rTMS over the left dlPFC enhances cortical excitability and monoaminergic tone, treating refractory depression.

questions.question: Which technique provides the highest spatial and temporal resolution simultaneously, but is restricted to animal models due to required genetic modification and fiber optic implantation?

options.text: Optogenetics
Scalp EEG
Clinical CT scans
Functional MRI

questions.explanation: Optogenetics delivers millisecond temporal control and single-cell/circuit-specific spatial resolution via light-gated opsins in model organisms.
